title: At 38, Tim Ream Aims to Anchor U.S. Defense and Ignite a Soccer Revolution at Home
summary: When the 2026 FIFA World Cup kicks off on June 11, it will be the first time the men's tournament is held on American soil since 1994. For Tim Ream, that earlier World Cup is a distant childhood memory—he was only 6 years old. Now 38, the Charlotte FC defender is poised to make his second World Cup roster, and he carries a dual mission: anchor the U.S. defense and finally prove that America can be a soccer nation. The U.S. Men's National Team faces immense pressure. After failing to qualify in 2018 and exiting in the Round of 16 in 2022, fans are hungry for a deep run. But Ream is confident. "I have no doubt in my mind that we can win in a knockout stage game," he told NPR. "I have no doubt that we can win multiple games in the knockout stages." Ream started all four U.S. matches in Qatar, playing every minute. He's the only current player with any memory of the 1994 World Cup, which sparked the creation of Major League Soccer. Now, he hopes 2026 will be an even bigger catalyst. "People want to believe that soccer in America is going to continue to grow," Ream said. "The biggest hope and dream would be to say we've inspired our own country of 330-plus million people, that we're inspiring the next generation of players." The final 26-man roster will be announced tomorrow. Ream, a former team captain, is ready for any role—starter, substitute, or veteran leader. His experience could be crucial for a squad that was the second-youngest in 2022. "At the last World Cup, none of us had played. We had one guy who had played in a World Cup previously," Ream said. "Now I think guys have a much better understanding of what it takes." For Ream, the tournament isn't just about wins and losses. It's about fostering a love for the game among American children—and finally silencing the naysayers who claim the U.S. will never be a soccer country.
why_it_matters: The 2026 World Cup outcome could reshape global perceptions of American soccer and either fuel or stall the sport's growth in the U.S., influencing funding, youth participation, and national identity.

background_read: The 1994 FIFA World Cup, hosted by the United States, set attendance records that still stand; it directly led to the founding of Major League Soccer (MLS) in 1996, giving the U.S. its first stable professional league.
Tim Ream spent most of his club career in England with Fulham and Bolton Wanderers before returning to the U.S. to play for Charlotte FC (a North Carolina expansion team that joined MLS in 2022).

The 2026 tournament will be co-hosted by the U.S., Canada, and Mexico, and will feature 48 teams for the first time — expanding the opportunity for smaller nations and increasing the number of matches.
The U.S. Men's National Team advanced to the quarterfinals in 2002 but has not won a knockout match since, amplifying pressure to deliver a breakout performance on home soil.

perspectives.description: Hosting the World Cup gives the U.S. a rare stage to showcase its rising talent, attract millions of new fans, and prove that soccer can stand alongside football, basketball, and baseball in the American sports landscape.

Doubters point out that the U.S. has repeatedly underperformed in men's soccer despite enormous resources, and an early exit would reinforce the belief that America will never truly be a soccer country.

Host nations often exceed expectations due to home advantage and investment; however, the U.S. faces structural challenges like a fragmented youth system compared to European academies. The 1994 precedent shows that one tournament alone can trigger a generation of growth — but success is not guaranteed.

A deep run could spark a surge in soccer participation and commercial investment, while a failure might cause momentum to fade. Regardless, the event will force the country to confront whether it is willing to treat soccer as a mainstream sport long-term.
